Then let me walk you through the ground floor layout first, and I will leave the renderings for the end.
That works. I will say now that my main concern is the distance from the loading bay to the storage area.
Thank you for saying it early. I was wondering whether the current distance works for your operation, or whether it costs you time on every trip.
It costs us time. About ninety seconds each way, and we do that forty times a shift.
That is a real number, and it changes the priority. We can address it by moving the door six metres, but the compromise is a narrower corridor on the north side.

Which of these would stop you working, and which would only annoy you?

For about ten years I said yes in design reviews, and I meant nothing by it. Somebody would show me a drawing and ask if I liked it. I am not a designer. Liking it is not my job, and saying no felt like criticising people who had worked for three months. So I said it looked good, and everybody went away happy. The worst one was a layout where a door was fine on the drawing and completely wrong for our forklifts, and I had said the layout was fine because nobody asked me about forklifts. Now the engineers I work with best ask me different questions. How many times a shift does your team make that trip. Where does the pallet go after it leaves the truck. What would you do if this door were closed for maintenance. I can answer those. I cannot answer do you like it, and when somebody asks me that, they get a polite yes and no information at all.

There is one habit that separates a review that works from a review that goes badly, and it has nothing to do with the drawings. Show the weakest part yourself, early. Most people do the opposite. They put the good views first, spend twenty minutes there, and hope nobody scrolls to the corner they are unsure about. The client always notices, and now two things are true: there is a problem, and you did not mention it. The second one is the expensive one. The other thing I would say is about concerns. When a client raises a concern, most engineers hear an attack, and they start defending the drawing. In my experience a concern is almost always a requirement that nobody wrote down. So the useful response is not a defence. It is a question: could you tell me what happens today, in the building you have now? Nine times out of ten the answer contains the constraint you were missing.

When a review ends, somebody usually sends a list of comments, and almost every list I have seen mixes two completely different things. Some of those comments are requirements: the turning circle of the forklift is what it is, and no amount of goodwill will make it smaller. Others are preferences: we would rather have the offices on the south side, because the view is better. Both are legitimate, but they are not the same, and the design team cannot tell them apart from the outside. So they either treat everything as fixed, which makes the design impossible, or they treat everything as negotiable, which makes us angry. There is one question that sorts the list in about two minutes, and I recommend asking it out loud at the end of every review. Which of these would stop you working, and which would only annoy you? People answer that honestly, because it gives them permission to say the second one.
